title: Decode String
prompt:
Given an encoded string `s`, return its decoded string. The encoding rule is `k[encoded_string]`, where `encoded_string` inside the square brackets is repeated exactly `k` times. `k` is guaranteed to be a positive integer.

Encodings can be nested, e.g. `3[a2[c]]` decodes to `accaccacc`. You may assume the input string is always valid, contains no extra whitespace, and square brackets are well-formed. Digits are only used for repeat counts `k`, never as part of the string to output.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters, digits, and square brackets '[]'
s is guaranteed to be a valid encoding
All integers in s are between 1 and 300
hints: Nested brackets mean you need to fully resolve an inner encoding before you know what to repeat for an outer one — that's a last-in-first-out dependency.
Use a stack that holds (previous_string_so_far, repeat_count) pairs, pushing a new frame whenever you see '[' and popping when you see ']'.
On ']', pop the count and previous string, then set current = previous + current * count — this correctly rebuilds the outer context after the inner bracket is fully decoded.

solution.approach: Walk the string maintaining a stack of (previous_string, repeat_count) frames plus a running current_string and current_number. Digits accumulate current_number. On '[', push (current_string, current_number) and reset both to build the bracketed segment fresh. On ']', pop the saved previous string and count, and set current_string = previous_string + current_string * count, splicing the fully-decoded inner segment back into its outer context. Regular letters just append to current_string. This correctly handles arbitrary nesting because each bracket level's context is preserved on the stack until its closing bracket.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) where n is the length of the fully decoded output
